items.stem: How are the elements arranged in the Periodic Table?
options: In alphabetical order of their symbols
In order of increasing nucleon number
In order of increasing proton number
items.answer: In order of increasing proton number
items.markingKey: Modern table: increasing proton (atomic) number; elements with similar properties fall in the same group.

items.stem: Explain why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
items.answer: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and reactions involve the outer electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same number of outer electrons; 1 mark: outer electrons determine reactions [2]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of electrons, why sodium forms Na⁺ ions but chlorine forms Cl⁻ ions.
items.answer: Sodium (2,8,1) loses its one outer electron to gain a full outer shell; chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to fill its outer shell.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Element X is in Group I and element Y is in Group VI. X is sodium and Y is oxygen. What is the formula of the compound they form?
items.answer: Na₂O
items.markingKey: sodium forms Na+, oxygen forms O2−; balance charges: Na₂O.

items.stem: Use the positions of potassium (2,8,8,1) and oxygen (2,6) in the Periodic Table to deduce the charges on their ions and the formula of the compound formed between them.
items.answer: K+ and O2−; K₂O
items.markingKey: 1 mark each ion charge; 1 mark formula K₂O [3]

items.stem: The table gives the electronic configurations of five elements (letters are not symbols): Q 2,8; R 2,5; T 2,8,5; X 2,2; Z 2,8,2. (a) Which elements are in the same period as Q? (b) Which elements are metals? Explain how you decided. (c) Predict the charge on the ion formed by T, if any.
items.answer: (a) R, X (b) X, Z: they have 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons (left of the table) and lose them to form positive ions. (c) -3
items.markingKey: (a) same number of shells [1] (b) 1 mark letters; 1 mark reason [2] (c) from number of outer electrons [1]

items.stem: Describe how the oxides of the elements change across Period 3 from sodium to sulfur.
items.answer: Oxides change from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂).
items.markingKey: 1 mark basic left; 1 mark acidic right; 1 mark amphoteric aluminium [3]

items.stem: What type of oxide is MgO, the oxide of magnesium?
items.answer: basic
items.markingKey: Across Period 3 oxides go basic → amphoteric → acidic; MgO is basic.

items.stem: Predict whether SO₂, the oxide of sulfur, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, with aqueous sodium hydroxide, or with both. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Reacts with alkali only: it is an acidic (non-metal) oxide.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: prediction; 1 mark: type of oxide linked to metallic/non-metallic character [2]

items.stem: The table gives the electronic configurations of five elements (letters are not symbols): Q 2,7; R 2,8,2; T 2,1; X 2,8,8; Z 2,8,7. (a) Which elements are metals? Explain how you decided. (b) Name the element X.
items.answer: (a) R, T: they have 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons (left of the table) and lose them to form positive ions. (b) argon
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark letters; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: How does the melting point of the Group I metals change down the group?
items.answer: It decreases
items.markingKey: Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C: metallic bonding weakens as atoms get larger.

items.stem: Explain why the reactivity of the Group I metals increases down the group.
items.answer: The outer electron is further from the nucleus (more shells, more shielding), so it is less strongly attracted and lost more easily.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more shells / further from nucleus; 1 mark: outer electron lost more easily [2]

items.stem: Explain why sodium floats on water while it reacts.
items.answer: Sodium has a lower density (0.97 g/cm³) than water (1.00 g/cm³).

items.stem: Caesium reacts with oxygen. Name the product(s) and write the balanced symbol equation.
items.answer: caesium oxide; 4Cs + O₂ → 2Cs₂O
items.markingKey: 1 mark name(s); 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced [3]

items.stem: Caesium reacts with water. Name the product(s) and write the balanced symbol equation. Include state symbols.
items.answer: caesium hydroxide and hydrogen; 2Cs + 2H₂O → 2CsOH + H₂
items.markingKey: 1 mark name(s); 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced ; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: Lithium reacts with oxygen. Name the product(s) and write the balanced symbol equation. Include state symbols.
items.answer: lithium oxide; 4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O
items.markingKey: 1 mark name(s); 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced ; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: An encyclopaedia lists the properties of caesium (proton number 55), a Group I element. (a) Predict how the melting point of caesium compares with that of potassium. (b) A 0.780 g piece of sodium is used. Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at r.t.p.
items.answer: (a) lower: melting point decreases down the group (b) 407 cm³

items.stem: An encyclopaedia lists the properties of potassium (proton number 19), a Group I element. (a) Describe what would be seen when potassium is added to water. (b) Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
items.answer: (a) reacts violently, melts, moves rapidly and the hydrogen burns with a lilac flame; the indicator turns purple/blue. (b) Potassium has more electron shells; its outer electron is further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted, so it is lost more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per observation, max [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Explain why all the Group I metals react in a similar way with water.
items.answer: Each has one outer electron, which is lost to form a 1+ ion; each forms a hydroxide and hydrogen.

items.stem: Explain why the solution turns universal indicator purple after lithium has reacted with water.
items.answer: Lithium hydroxide is formed, which is a soluble alkali (OH⁻ ions), so the pH is high.

items.stem: Explain why sodium melts into a ball when it reacts with water but lithium does not.
items.answer: The reaction is exothermic; sodium has a low melting point (98 °C) and the reaction is fast enough to melt it; lithium reacts more slowly and has a higher melting point (181 °C).

items.stem: 1.17 g of sodium reacts with excess water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure, in cm³. (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
items.answer: 610 cm³

items.stem: An encyclopaedia lists the properties of potassium (proton number 19), a Group I element. (a) Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why potassium is less reactive than rubidium. (b) Suggest one safety precaution needed for this demonstration.
items.answer: (a) Potassium has fewer electron shells; its outer electron is closer to the nucleus and more strongly attracted, so it is lost less easily. (b) Use a very small piece / safety screen / goggles / tongs, not fingers.

items.stem: Sofia watches a teacher add a small piece of potassium to a trough of water containing a few drops of universal indicator. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction with water. (b) Predict how the melting point of potassium compares with that of caesium. (c) Suggest one safety precaution needed for this demonstration. (d) State the formula of the ion formed by potassium and explain its charge.
items.answer: (a) 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ (b) higher: melting point decreases down the group (c) Use a very small piece / safety screen / goggles / tongs, not fingers. (d) K⁺: it loses its single outer electron.

items.stem: What is the colour and state of bromine at room temperature?
items.answer: red-brown liquid
items.markingKey: Cl₂ pale yellow-green gas; Br₂ red-brown liquid; I₂ grey-black solid.

items.stem: Explain why the reactivity of the halogens decreases down Group VII.
items.answer: Atoms get larger with more shells, so the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly; the atom gains an electron less easily.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more shells/larger atom; 1 mark: electron gained less easily [2]

items.stem: Explain why bromine water does not react with aqueous potassium chloride.
items.answer: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace chloride ions.

items.stem: Aqueous chlorine is added to aqueous potassium bromide. Predict whether a reaction occurs. If it does, describe the colour change and write the balanced symbol equation.
items.answer: Yes — the colourless solution turns orange as bromine is formed. Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reaction because chlorine is more reactive; 1 mark: colour; 1 mark: equation [3]

items.stem: Aqueous bromine is added to aqueous potassium chloride. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction: bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace the chloride ion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no reaction; 1 mark: reactivity reason [2]

items.stem: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Use the trends in the group to predict its state and colour, giving a reason.
items.answer: A black solid (darker than iodine, solid because melting/boiling points increase down the group).
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark trend reason [2]

items.stem: Samuel adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: bromine + potassium iodide; chlorine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium chloride; bromine + potassium chloride. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard. (c) Identify the reducing agent in the first mixture that reacts.
items.answer: (a) bromine + iodide; chlorine + iodide (b) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic. (c) iodide ions (I⁻)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Omar adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: chlorine + potassium iodide; chlorine + potassium bromide; iodine + potassium bromide; bromine + potassium iodide. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Describe the colour change for the first mixture that reacts. (c) Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (d) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) chlorine + iodide; chlorine + bromide; bromine + iodide (b) the colourless solution turns brown as iodine is formed (c) chlorine > bromine > iodine (d) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: How does the reactivity of the halogens change down Group VII?
items.answer: It decreases
items.markingKey: F > Cl > Br > I: the atom gains an electron less easily as it gets larger.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction between chlorine and potassium bromide is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Chlorine gains electrons (reduced) to form Cl⁻; bromide ions lose electrons (oxidised) to form Br₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why all halogens have similar chemical properties.
items.answer: Each atom has seven outer electrons and gains one electron to form a 1− ion.

items.stem: A student says, "Iodine is more reactive than bromine because it is a solid." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Physical state does not determine reactivity; iodine is less reactive because its larger atoms gain an electron less easily.

items.stem: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Use the trends in the group to predict its boiling point, giving a reason.
items.answer: Higher than that of iodine (184 °C): boiling point increases down the group.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark trend reason [2]

items.stem: Noah adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: chlorine + potassium iodide; bromine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium chloride; bromine + potassium chloride. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (c) Identify the reducing agent in the first mixture that reacts.
items.answer: (a) chlorine + iodide; bromine + iodide (b) chlorine > bromine > iodine (c) iodide ions (I⁻)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which property is typical of transition elements but not of Group I metals?
options: They react vigorously with cold water
items.answer: They form coloured compounds
items.markingKey: Transition elements: high density, high m.p., coloured compounds, variable oxidation numbers, catalysts.

items.stem: Explain why transition elements are useful in industry as catalysts.
items.answer: They (or their compounds) speed up reactions without being used up, so less energy/lower temperatures are needed and costs fall.

items.stem: Compare the physical properties of the Group I metals and the transition elements.
items.answer: Group I: soft, low density, low melting points; transition elements: hard, high density, high melting points.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each comparison, max [3]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of chromium in CrCl₃ and hence name the compound using a Roman numeral.
items.answer: +3; chromium(III) compound
items.markingKey: Oxidation numbers in a compound sum to zero; O = −2, Cl = −1, K = +1, SO₄ = −2, NO₃ = −1, OH = −1 [1]; chromium = +3 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of vanadium in V₂O₅ and hence name the compound using a Roman numeral.
items.answer: +5; vanadium(V) compound
items.markingKey: Oxidation numbers in a compound sum to zero; O = −2, Cl = −1, K = +1, SO₄ = −2, NO₃ = −1, OH = −1 [1]; vanadium = +5 [1]

items.stem: A museum display shows minerals that contain vanadium, including one with the formula V₂O₅. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of vanadium in V₂O₅. (b) Vanadium also forms VO₂. Explain what this shows about transition elements. (c) Vanadium(V) oxide is used in the Contact process to make sulfuric acid. State what is meant by a catalyst.
items.answer: (a) +5 (b) They have variable oxidation numbers: here +4 compared with +5. (c) A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged at the end.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by "variable oxidation number", using iron as an example.
items.answer: An element can form ions with different charges in different compounds, e.g. Fe²⁺ in iron(II) sulfate and Fe³⁺ in iron(III) chloride.

items.stem: Data for three metals are given. J: density 8.96 g/cm³, melting point 1085 °C, compounds blue or green; L: density 0.86 g/cm³, melting point 63 °C, compounds white; M: density 0.97 g/cm³, melting point 98 °C, compounds white. Deduce which metal is a transition element and give two pieces of evidence from the data.
items.answer: J (copper): high density, high melting point and coloured compounds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct letter; 1 mark each for two pieces of evidence [3]

items.stem: Data for three metals are given. J: density 8.9 g/cm³, melting point 1495 °C, compounds pink or blue; L: density 1.55 g/cm³, melting point 842 °C, compounds white; M: density 1.74 g/cm³, melting point 650 °C, compounds white. Deduce which metal is a transition element and give two pieces of evidence from the data.
items.answer: J (cobalt): high density, high melting point and coloured compounds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct letter; 1 mark each for two pieces of evidence [3]

items.stem: A pigment manufacturer in Dubai uses compounds of nickel, such as NiO. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of nickel in NiO. (b) Name NiO using a Roman numeral. (c) Vanadium(V) oxide is used in the Contact process to make sulfuric acid. State what is meant by a catalyst. (d) Predict, with a reason, whether NiO is likely to be white or coloured.
items.answer: (a) +2 (b) nickel(II) oxide (c) A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged at the end. (d) Coloured: compounds of transition elements are usually coloured.

items.stem: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
options: They have full outer electron shells
items.answer: They have full outer electron shells
items.markingKey: A full outer shell is stable, so noble gas atoms do not lose, gain or share electrons.

items.stem: Noble gases exist as
items.answer: single atoms (monatomic)
items.markingKey: Their atoms are stable, so they do not bond to each other.

items.stem: Explain why argon is used to fill filament lamps instead of air.
items.answer: Argon is unreactive, so the very hot tungsten filament does not react (oxidise) and burn away, as it would in oxygen.

items.stem: The boiling points of some noble gases are: helium −269 °C; neon −246 °C; argon −186 °C. Predict the boiling point of krypton and state its physical state at room temperature. Explain why it does not react with fluorine easily.
items.answer: About −153 °C (any value between −166 and −106 °C); gas; full outer shell ({tgt[3]}) so it is very unreactive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction following trend; 1 mark gas; 1 mark full outer shell [3]

items.stem: Air contains small amounts of noble gases including xenon and helium. (a) Give the electronic configuration of xenon. (b) Explain why xenon is suitable for bright car headlamps and camera flashes.
items.answer: (a) 2,8,18,18,8 (b) It gives an intense light when electricity passes.

items.stem: Which gas is used to fill weather balloons?
items.answer: helium
items.markingKey: Helium has a low density and is non-flammable.

items.stem: A balloon is filled with 9.60 dm³ of helium at r.t.p. Calculate the mass of helium in the balloon (Ar He = 4). The same volume of air (mean Mr 29) has a mass of 11.6 g. Use this to explain why a helium-filled balloon rises.
items.answer: 1.60 g — it is less dense than air.
items.markingKey: n = 9.60/24 = 0.400 mol [1]; mass = 0.400 × 4 = 1.60 g [1]; compares mass/density with air [1]

items.stem: What do elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have in common?
options: The same number of outer-shell electrons
The same number of electron shells
items.answer: The same number of outer-shell electrons
items.markingKey: Group number (I–VII) = number of outer electrons; this gives similar chemical properties.

items.stem: Explain why helium is placed in Group VIII even though it has only two outer electrons.
items.answer: Its outer (first) shell is full, so like the other noble gases it is unreactive.

items.stem: Element X is in Group I and element Y is in Group VI. X is sodium and Y is sulfur. What is the formula of the compound they form?
items.answer: Na₂S
items.markingKey: sodium forms Na+, sulfur forms S2−; balance charges: Na₂S.

items.stem: The table gives the electronic configurations of five elements (letters are not symbols): Q 2,2; R 2,8,7; T 2,8,5; X 2,1; Z 2,8,8,1. (a) Which elements are metals? Explain how you decided. (b) State the group and period of R. (c) Which two elements would have similar chemical properties? Explain.
items.answer: (a) Q, X, Z: they have 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons (left of the table) and lose them to form positive ions. (b) Group VII, Period 3 (c) X and Z: same number of outer electrons (same group).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark letters; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which gas is produced when sodium reacts with water?
items.answer: hydrogen
items.markingKey: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why sodium floats on water while it reacts. (b) Explain why the solution turns universal indicator purple after lithium has reacted with water.
items.answer: (a) Sodium has a lower density (0.97 g/cm³) than water (1.00 g/cm³). (b) Lithium hydroxide is formed, which is a soluble alkali (OH⁻ ions), so the pH is high.

items.stem: The densities of some Group I metals are: lithium 0.53 g/cm³; sodium 0.97 g/cm³; potassium 0.86 g/cm³. Predict the density of rubidium and describe how its reaction with water would compare with that of potassium.
items.answer: About 1.53 g/cm³ (accept a value consistent with the trend: higher than 0.97); it reacts more violently/explosively than potassium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: prediction consistent with trend (density generally increases down the group); 1 mark: more reactive (explosive) [2]

items.stem: 0.690 g of potassium reacts with excess water: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure, in cm³. (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
items.answer: 212 cm³

items.stem: A video from a laboratory in Auckland shows potassium and rubidium being added to separate troughs of cold water. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction with water. (b) State the formula of the ion formed by potassium and explain its charge.
items.answer: (a) 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ (b) K⁺: it loses its single outer electron.

items.stem: What is the physical state of chlorine at room temperature and pressure?
items.answer: gas
items.markingKey: chlorine: pale yellow-green gas.

items.stem: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂. Identify the oxidising agent and the species that is oxidised in this reaction, explaining your answer in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: chlorine (Cl₂) is the oxidising agent — it gains electrons and is reduced to Cl⁻; the iodide ions (I⁻) are oxidised — they lose electrons to form I₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark oxidising agent; 1 mark species oxidised; 1 mark electron transfer explanation [3]

items.stem: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Use the trends in the group to predict its reaction with potassium iodide, giving a reason.
items.answer: No reaction: astatine is less reactive than iodine so cannot displace iodide ions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark trend reason [2]

items.stem: Ethan adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: chlorine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium bromide; iodine + potassium chloride; bromine + potassium iodide. (a) Explain this order in terms of the electronic structure of the atoms. (b) Identify the reducing agent in the first mixture that reacts.
items.answer: (a) Down the group atoms have more shells; the nucleus attracts an extra electron less strongly, so the halogen gains electrons less readily. (b) iodide ions (I⁻)

items.stem: Omar adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: bromine + potassium chloride; chlorine + potassium bromide; iodine + potassium chloride; bromine + potassium iodide. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (c) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) chlorine + bromide; bromine + iodide (b) chlorine > bromine > iodine (c) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Explain how you could tell from appearance alone that a compound probably contains a transition element.
items.answer: Transition element compounds are usually coloured (e.g. blue copper(II) sulfate); compounds of Group I and II metals are usually white or colourless.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain what is meant by "variable oxidation number", using iron as an example. (b) Compare the physical properties of the Group I metals and the transition elements.
items.answer: (a) An element can form ions with different charges in different compounds, e.g. Fe²⁺ in iron(II) sulfate and Fe³⁺ in iron(III) chloride. (b) Group I: soft, low density, low melting points; transition elements: hard, high density, high melting points.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each comparison, max [3]

items.stem: Data for three metals are given. J: density 1.55 g/cm³, melting point 842 °C, compounds white; L: density 7.87 g/cm³, melting point 1538 °C, compounds green or brown; M: density 1.74 g/cm³, melting point 650 °C, compounds white. Deduce which metal is a transition element and give two pieces of evidence from the data.
items.answer: L (iron): high density, high melting point and coloured compounds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct letter; 1 mark each for two pieces of evidence [3]

items.stem: Explain why helium is safer than hydrogen for filling airships.
items.answer: Both have low density, but helium is unreactive and does not burn, whereas hydrogen is flammable/explosive in air.

items.stem: A balloon is filled with 9.60 dm³ of neon at r.t.p. Calculate the mass of neon in the balloon (Ar Ne = 20).

Felix reads that xenon (proton number 54) is used for bright car headlamps and camera flashes. (a) Give the electronic configuration of xenon. (b) State why xenon is described as monatomic. (c) Explain why xenon is suitable for bright car headlamps and camera flashes. (d) Suggest how noble gases are obtained from the air.
items.answer: (a) 2,8,18,18,8 (b) It exists as single atoms, not molecules. (c) It gives an intense light when electricity passes. (d) By fractional distillation of liquid air.

items.stem: The period number of an element tells you
options: the number of occupied electron shells
items.answer: the number of occupied electron shells
items.markingKey: Period = number of shells containing electrons.

items.stem: Explain why the elements in a period do not have similar properties to each other.
items.answer: Each has a different number of outer electrons, so they react differently (metals on the left, non-metals on the right).

items.stem: Predict whether MgO, the oxide of magnesium, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, with aqueous sodium hydroxide, or with both. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Reacts with acid only: it is a basic (metal) oxide.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: prediction; 1 mark: type of oxide linked to metallic/non-metallic character [2]

items.stem: The table gives the electronic configurations of five elements (letters are not symbols): Q 2,8,8,2; R 2,8,8,1; T 2,8,6; X 2,8,2; Z 2,7. (a) Which elements are metals? Explain how you decided. (b) State the group and period of R. (c) Predict the charge on the ion formed by T, if any. (d) Name the element X.
items.answer: (a) Q, R, X: they have 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons (left of the table) and lose them to form positive ions. (b) Group I, Period 4 (c) -2 (d) magnesium
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark letters; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [2] (c) from number of outer electrons [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Why are Group I metals stored under oil?
options: To prevent them reacting with oxygen and water vapour in the air
items.answer: To prevent them reacting with oxygen and water vapour in the air
items.markingKey: They are very reactive; oil keeps air and moisture away.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why sodium melts into a ball when it reacts with water but lithium does not. (b) Explain why sodium floats on water while it reacts.
items.answer: (a) The reaction is exothermic; sodium has a low melting point (98 °C) and the reaction is fast enough to melt it; lithium reacts more slowly and has a higher melting point (181 °C). (b) Sodium has a lower density (0.97 g/cm³) than water (1.00 g/cm³).

items.stem: The melting points of some Group I metals are: lithium 181 °C; sodium 98 °C; potassium 63 °C; rubidium 39 °C. Predict the melting point of caesium and describe how its reaction with water would compare with that of rubidium.
items.answer: About 29 °C (accept a value consistent with the trend: lower than 39 °C); it reacts more violently/explosively than rubidium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: prediction consistent with trend (melting point decreases down the group); 1 mark: more reactive (explosive) [2]

items.stem: An encyclopaedia lists the properties of rubidium (proton number 37), a Group I element. (a) Predict how the melting point of rubidium compares with that of sodium. (b) State the formula of the ion formed by rubidium and explain its charge.
items.answer: (a) lower: melting point decreases down the group (b) Rb⁺: it loses its single outer electron.

items.stem: Nadia watches a teacher add a small piece of lithium to a trough of water containing a few drops of universal indicator. (a) Describe what would be seen when lithium is added to water. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction with water.
items.answer: (a) fizzes steadily and floats; it does not melt; the indicator turns purple/blue. (b) 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per observation, max [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State how the melting and boiling points of the halogens change down the group. (b) How does the reactivity of the halogens change down Group VII?
items.answer: (a) They increase. (b) It decreases
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) F > Cl > Br > I: the atom gains an electron less easily as it gets larger.

items.stem: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Identify the oxidising agent and the species that is oxidised in this reaction, explaining your answer in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: bromine (Br₂) is the oxidising agent — it gains electrons and is reduced to Br⁻; the iodide ions (I⁻) are oxidised — they lose electrons to form I₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark oxidising agent; 1 mark species oxidised; 1 mark electron transfer explanation [3]

items.stem: Aqueous bromine is added to aqueous sodium chloride. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction: bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace the chloride ion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no reaction; 1 mark: reactivity reason [2]

items.stem: Isla adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: iodine + potassium bromide; chlorine + potassium bromide; chlorine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium chloride. (a) Write the ionic equation for the first mixture that reacts. (b) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ (b) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.

items.stem: Leila adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: chlorine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium bromide; bromine + potassium chloride; chlorine + potassium bromide. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Describe the colour change for the first mixture that reacts. (c) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) chlorine + iodide; chlorine + bromide (b) the colourless solution turns brown as iodine is formed (c) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Compare the physical properties of the Group I metals and the transition elements. (b) Explain how you could tell from appearance alone that a compound probably contains a transition element.
items.answer: (a) Group I: soft, low density, low melting points; transition elements: hard, high density, high melting points. (b) Transition element compounds are usually coloured (e.g. blue copper(II) sulfate); compounds of Group I and II metals are usually white or colourless.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each comparison, max [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how you could tell from appearance alone that a compound probably contains a transition element. (b) Explain why transition elements are useful in industry as catalysts.
items.answer: (a) Transition element compounds are usually coloured (e.g. blue copper(II) sulfate); compounds of Group I and II metals are usually white or colourless. (b) They (or their compounds) speed up reactions without being used up, so less energy/lower temperatures are needed and costs fall.

items.stem: Data for three metals are given. J: density 8.96 g/cm³, melting point 1085 °C, compounds blue or green; L: density 0.97 g/cm³, melting point 98 °C, compounds white; M: density 1.74 g/cm³, melting point 650 °C, compounds white. Deduce which metal is a transition element and give two pieces of evidence from the data.
items.answer: J (copper): high density, high melting point and coloured compounds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct letter; 1 mark each for two pieces of evidence [3]

items.stem: Explain, using electronic configurations, why neon does not form compounds but sodium does.
items.answer: Neon (2,8) has a full outer shell so it is stable; sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron easily to reach a full outer shell.

items.stem: A balloon is filled with 3.60 dm³ of argon at r.t.p. Calculate the mass of argon in the balloon (Ar Ar = 40).

Air contains small amounts of noble gases including xenon and argon. (a) State why xenon is described as monatomic. (b) Explain why xenon is suitable for bright car headlamps and camera flashes. (c) Predict whether xenon has a higher or lower boiling point than argon. (d) Suggest how noble gases are obtained from the air.
items.answer: (a) It exists as single atoms, not molecules. (b) It gives an intense light when electricity passes. (c) higher (d) By fractional distillation of liquid air.
